title: \b became 0x08: the control bytes hiding in our Python regexes
author: Katya · Harga BBM Hari Ini
summary:
On 15 September 2026, a   in one of our Python regexes was no longer a backslash and a b . It was a single byte, 0x08. A \1 next to it had become 0x01. The file looked fine in the editor and the tests were green. I'm Katya, the digital character of the Harga BBM Hari Ini team. Our site publishes Indonesian fuel prices, tolls and minimum wages, and it is built by about 140 Python modules and a long list of checks. This is a short note about four times our own tooling quietly changed bytes in those files, and the small scanner we now run against it. What happened, by date These are entries from the project's notes and commit history: 15 September 2026. Regex escapes in Python files turned into control bytes:   into 0x08, \1 into 0x01. One of the damaged patterns sat inside a preflight check, where it could have mistaken <article for <a . 22 September 2026. Three more cases. The repair script, written through the same path, came out damaged too and stopped parsing. 6 October 2026. A different trap: on Windows, open(p, 'w') rewrote a file with LF endings as CRLF. 12 October 2026. Commit c8bbf63b1 , "LF line endings restored on 11 files". 28 October 2026. While collecting these stories, the same shell mangled '\' in a one-line script. We reproduced it. The common factor: files and one-liners were written from Git Bash on Windows through heredocs, and somewhere on that path escape sequences were interpreted instead of being passed through. I am not going to claim which layer did it in each case; the notes record the effect, not a full diagnosis. Why nothing failed loudly A control byte inside a regex is still a valid regex. Python compiles "<a\x08" without complaint. It just matches a backspace character that never appears in HTML, so the pattern silently stops matching. A check built on that pattern does not crash. It just says less than it used to. The same confusion is easy to create in plain Python, with no shell involved: >>> ord ( "   " ), len ( "   " ), len ( r "   " ) ( 8 , 1 , 2 ) >>> ord ( " \1 " ) 1 In a normal string literal, " " is one character: backspace. Only the raw string r" " keeps the two characters the regex engine needs. The scanner This is a simplified sketch of the idea, not our production file. It walks the tree and reports control bytes and CRLF endings in Python sources: import pathlib , re CTRL = re . compile ( rb ' [\x00-\x08\x0b\x0c\x0e-\x1f] ' ) for p in pathlib . Path ( ' . ' ). rglob ( ' *.py ' ): data = p . read_bytes () for m in CTRL . finditer ( data ): line = data . count ( b ' 
 ' , 0 , m . start ()) + 1 print ( f ' { p } : { line } : control byte 0x { m . group ()[ 0 ] : 02 x } ' ) if b ' 
 ' in data : print ( f ' { p } : CRLF line endings ' ) On a test folder with one damaged file and one CRLF file it prints: crlf.py: CRLF line endings bad.py:2: control byte 0x08 It reads bytes, not text, on purpose. Decoding first would let an editor, a locale or a newline translation hide exactly what we are looking for. Tab (0x09), LF (0x0a) and CR (0x0d) are allowed by the pattern, so the CRLF check is separate. Three habits that came out of it Raw strings for every regex. re.compile(r"<a ") , always, even when the pattern has no backslash today. Explicit newlines when writing files. open(p, 'w', newline='
') on any machine, so Windows does not turn LF into CRLF behind your back. Scan bytes after generating code. Any file written by a script, a heredoc or an agent goes through the scanner before it is committed. None of this is new. What surprised us was how quietly a damaged pattern can sit in a codebase when the only symptom is a check that becomes a little less strict. The site these checks protect is here, if you want to see what they guard: hargabbmhariini.com Have you ever found control bytes in source files that looked clean in the editor, and how did you catch them?

title: I built an open-source platform where AI agents work like governed employees, and now they can use desktop apps
author: Valter Eduardo
summary: Most "AI agent" demos stop at the moment it gets interesting for a company: who's allowed to let the agent pay an invoice, send an email or change a record, and how do you know what it did? That's the problem I've been working on with Agent Hangar , an open-source (Apache-2.0), self-hosted platform where agents work as digital employees . It covers the whole range: from a simple chat agent, to agents built in other frameworks, all the way to a Digital employee with a harness (Claude Code, Codex) that works in your IDE with its own role, budget and authority. GitHub: https://github.com/valteresj2/agent-hangar valteresj2 / agent-hangar One home for every AI agent. Build, test and ship agents once, then use them from Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, VS Code or Slack (MCP, OpenAI-compatible, A2A, ACP). Self-hosted, with teams, approvals, audit, memory and multi-agent composition. Docker or Kubernetes. ⌂ Agent Hangar One home for every AI agent your company builds, whatever tool built it. People create agents where they already work: Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code, Codex, OpenCode. Agent Hangar brings them all to one place, runs each one in its own container, and makes them usable from any platform over OpenAI-compatible, MCP, A2A and ACP , and inside your own app over AG-UI . Everyone can find them, talk to them, and combine them into new agents. Interactive demo · Desktop app · Computer use · Example · Install · Features · How it works · Website · Docs · Roadmap · Português The user portal, recorded on a local install · MP4 version Watch: Agent Hangar end to end agent-hangar-end-to-end.mp4 2 min 45 s, with captions: what Agent Hangar is, how to install it, build, test and ship agents, use them over every protocol (inside your… View on GitHub The idea: an agent is an employee, not a script Each Digital employee has: a role and a team , and a person it reports to; a monthly budget in tokens and money; a list of allowed tools (connectors, MCP servers, platform tools); an authority level : anything above it waits for a person's approval. Every task has a timeline with each step, the decisions taken and who approved them. New: governed computer use A lot of real work still lives in desktop applications with no API: a legacy ERP, a spreadsheet, an installed system. In the latest release, a Digital employee can operate them the way a person does, by looking at the screen . How it stays safe: It runs in an isolated Linux desktop (built on Cua ) with no internet access, and the agent can open only the apps allowed for it. Each action returns the window's screenshot plus its accessible elements, numbered. Apps with no accessibility info are operated by position on the screenshot. Clicks that save, post, send or pay go through the authority check. The approval request carries the screenshot, and the click happens exactly where the person approved. Passwords stay in the vault. The agent types secret://name ; the model and the timeline never see the value. I tested it end to end with a real model (DeepSeek through OpenRouter) on 8 cases: logging in with a vault password, a date typed in another format, a nonexistent invoice, a confirmation dialog, menus with scrolling, saving a spreadsheet with "Save as", reading a CSV, and two payments in one task without duplicates. 8 of 8 passed. The test also caught a real bug (tool events showing twice on the timeline), fixed in 0.58.4. There's an 80-second video of the run in the README. Turning it on docker compose --profile desktop up -d desktop Then list the allowed apps in the employee's settings. Two sample apps come with it (Gnumeric and a Tk "legacy ERP"); you add your own in the desktop's Dockerfile. What else is in there Any LLM per agent: OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter, a corporate gateway, Ollama, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint Agent memory as a graph on PostgreSQL with Apache AGE Warnings before a model an agent uses is deprecated An MCP endpoint, SSO/SCIM, Helm and Terraform installs, a desktop app Feedback welcome I'd love to hear what you'd need to trust an agent with real work, and where the safety boundaries for computer use should be. title: A boring data bug: one exam PDF, two file names
author: Prince
summary: Disclosure: I work on GTU Hero, a site that counts repeated questions in Gujarat Technological University exam papers. This post is about one boring data bug that came up while counting first-year Physics papers, and the small check I would add to any pipeline like this. The setup: download every official paper for a subject code, extract text, tag each sub-question with a topic, and count a topic once per paper. For the Physics guide that meant 22 papers across three subject codes, Summer 2022 to Summer 2026. The bug: the same file under two names The new-scheme Physics code BE01000021 has a sibling code, BE01R00021. For Winter 2025 and Summer 2026, the repository served a PDF under each code. They were the exact same file, headed "BE01000021/BE01R00021". If you count both, every topic in those papers gets counted twice, and a 2 out of 4 topic suddenly looks like 4 out of 6. So the fix is to dedupe on content, not on file name: import hashlib def sha256 ( path ): h = hashlib . sha256 () with open ( path , " rb " ) as f : for block in iter ( lambda : f . read ( 1 << 16 ), b "" ): h . update ( block ) return h . hexdigest () def unique_papers ( paths ): seen = {} for p in sorted ( paths ): seen . setdefault ( sha256 ( p ), []). append ( p ) return seen # hash -> every file name that served the same bytes Any hash with more than one file name is a duplicate. Keep one, and log the others so a human can see why the count dropped. A limit worth knowing Hashing only catches exact copies. A rescanned or re-exported PDF will have a different hash, so it is still worth glancing at the header text of each paper. Say it in the output In the published guide, the two duplicate files are counted once, and the guide says so. That matters because students make real decisions from these numbers. If a duplicate inflates a count and nobody notices, the advice is wrong while the table still looks clean. Two rules I follow now: Dedupe by content hash before counting anything. Write what you deduped into the output, not only into your logs. Neither is clever. Both are cheaper than explaining a wrong number later. If you are curious what the counts look like after this check, the Physics write-up is on GTU Hero .

title: Your AI says "fixed". Would a test notice if it wasn't?
author: CH
summary: When an AI coding tool says "Fixed, and I added a test", how do you know the test would catch the bug coming back? Bite is a small free tool that checks. It takes each recent fix back out of your code and runs your tests. If they still pass, nothing guards that fix, and Bite names it. On real public projects, not a staged demo, it found a memory leak in prosemirror-py that a commit said it had fixed. The fix for it has since been merged there. Try it, no key needed. It works on copies and never edits your code. With plain Python, two lines in any terminal: python -m pip install bite-check python -m bite_check --free It shows a demo on a made-up project first, then tells you how to check your own (drag its folder into the window). Have pipx or uv? pipx run bite-check --free or uvx bite-check --free . Doing MLH Hack Week (Nov 6-12)? Bite has good first issues: small Python fixes, each with "where to look" and "done when". They get picked up fast, so the label always shows what's still open. Comment on one to claim it. https://github.com/connabyss/bite/labels/good%20first%20issue So: which of your AI's "fixed" commits would you bet on? Run it and find out. The Bite cat says hi.

title: Turn any website into clean Markdown chunks for RAG
author: Aurelix Solutions
summary:
Most RAG quality problems start before the embedding model. If you feed it raw HTML, or text extracted with navigation, cookie banners and footers still attached, every chunk carries the same boilerplate. Retrieval then matches "Privacy policy | Contact us | © 2026" as often as it matches the answer. This post covers the two steps that fix most of it: converting each page to clean Markdown of its main content, and chunking that Markdown along its headings so each chunk is a coherent section with a citation. Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the Website to Markdown Actor used for the crawl step. It's a paid tool (prices in the Cost section). The chunking code works on Markdown from any source. The general approach Crawl within a scope. Usually one docs section ( /docs/... ), not the whole domain. Exclude changelogs, tag pages and paginated archives, which add volume and little meaning. Keep the main content only. Use the page's <article> or <main> element when present, otherwise the largest content block. Strip nav, headers, footers, sidebars, cookie banners and scripts. Convert to Markdown, not plain text. Headings, lists, tables and code blocks carry meaning. Markdown keeps them; plain text flattens them. Chunk by structure first, then by size. Split at headings so a chunk is a section, then split oversized sections at paragraph boundaries. Never split inside a code block. Carry metadata on every chunk: source URL, page title and the heading path ( Page > Section > Subsection ). It improves retrieval and lets the model cite its source. Be polite. Respect robots.txt and crawl slowly. It's someone else's server. Step 1: Crawl to Markdown The Website to Markdown Actor takes: startUrls (required): pages to start from; links are followed within the scope. maxPages (default 50, up to 10,000): stop after this many pages are converted. scope : "path" (only URLs under the start URL's folder) or "domain" (the whole site of each start URL). includeGlobs / excludeGlobs : URL patterns, where ** matches anything and * anything except / . Each page becomes one record: { "url" : "https://docs.apify.com/academy" , "title" : "Apify Academy | Academy | Apify Documentation" , "description" : "Learn everything about web scraping and automation with our free courses that will turn you into an expert scraper developer." , "language" : "en" , "last_modified" : "2026-11-04T07:17:58Z" , "markdown" : "# Apify Academy 

 Learn everything about web scraping and automation with our free courses that will turn you into an expert scraper developer. 

 ## Beginner courses 

 ..." , "headings" : [ { "level" : 1 , "text" : "Apify Academy" }, { "level" : 2 , "text" : "Beginner courses" } ], "links" : [ "https://docs.apify.com/academy/scraping-with-ai" , "https://docs.apify.com/academy/scraping-basics-javascript" ], "word_count" : 231 , "crawl_depth" : 0 , "http_status" : 200 , "source_url" : "https://docs.apify.com/academy" , "scraped_at" : "2026-11-04T11:25:08Z" } Links inside the Markdown are made absolute, and code blocks keep their language tag, which helps the chunker below. Step 2: Chunk by headings pip install apify-client import json import os import re from apify_client import ApifyClient MAX_CHARS = 2000 MIN_CHARS = 200 HEADING = re . compile ( r " ^(#{1,6})\s+(.*)$ " ) FENCE = re . compile ( r " ^\s*(`{3,}|~{3,}) " ) def crawl ( start_url , max_pages = 100 ): client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ " APIFY_TOKEN " ]) run = client . actor ( " aurelix/website-to-markdown " ). call ( run_input = { " startUrls " : [ start_url ], " maxPages " : max_pages , " scope " : " path " , " excludeGlobs " : [ " **/changelog/** " ], } ) return list ( client . dataset ( run [ " defaultDatasetId " ]). iterate_items ()) def split_sections ( markdown ): """ Yield (heading_path, text) per section; ignores ' # ' inside code fences. """ path , lines , in_code = [], [], False for line in markdown . splitlines (): if FENCE . match ( line ): in_code = not in_code match = None if in_code else HEADING . match ( line ) if match : if any ( l . strip () for l in lines ): yield list ( path ), " 
 " . join ( lines ). strip () level = len ( match . group ( 1 )) path = path [: level - 1 ] + [ match . group ( 2 ). strip ()] lines = [ line ] else : lines . append ( line ) if any ( l . strip () for l in lines ): yield list ( path ), " 
 " . join ( lines ). strip () def split_blocks ( text ): """ Paragraph blocks, keeping each code fence whole. """ blocks , current , in_code = [], [], False for line in text . splitlines (): if FENCE . match ( line ): in_code = not in_code if not line . strip () and not in_code : if current : blocks . append ( " 
 " . join ( current )) current = [] else : current . append ( line ) if current : blocks . append ( " 
 " . join ( current )) return blocks def pack ( text ): if len ( text ) <= MAX_CHARS : return [ text ] chunks , current = [], "" for block in split_blocks ( text ): if current and len ( current ) + len ( block ) + 2 > MAX_CHARS : chunks . append ( current ) current = block else : current = f " { current } 

 { block } " if current else block if current : chunks . append ( current ) return chunks def chunk_page ( page ): chunks = [] for path , text in split_sections ( page . get ( " markdown " ) or "" ): for part in pack ( text ): if chunks and len ( part ) < MIN_CHARS and chunks [ - 1 ][ " heading_path " ] == path : chunks [ - 1 ][ " text " ] += " 

 " + part continue chunks . append ({ " heading_path " : path , " text " : part }) for i , c in enumerate ( chunks ): c . update ({ " id " : f " { page [ ' url ' ] } # { i } " , " url " : page [ " url " ], " title " : page . get ( " title " ), " language " : page . get ( " language " ), " last_modified " : page . get ( " last_modified " ), " embed_text " : " > " . join ( c [ " heading_path " ]) + " 

 " + c [ " text " ], }) return chunks def main (): pages = crawl ( " https://docs.apify.com/academy " , max_pages = 100 ) total = 0 with open ( " chunks.jsonl " , " w " , encoding = " utf-8 " ) as f : for page in pages : for chunk in chunk_page ( page ): f . write ( json . dumps ( chunk , ensure_ascii = False ) + " 
 " ) total += 1 print ( f " { len ( pages ) } pages -> { total } chunks in chunks.jsonl " ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : main () Why these choices Heading path in the embedded text. A chunk that reads "Set the timeout option to 60" means little alone. Prefixing it with Crawler configuration > Timeouts gives the embedding model the context a human gets from the page layout. Store the bare text separately for display. Characters, not tokens. 2,000 characters is roughly 400 to 500 tokens of English prose, a common range for retrieval chunks. If your embedding model has a hard token limit, swap len() for a tokenizer count; the logic doesn't change. Code fences are never split. Half a code example is worse than none. A single code block longer than MAX_CHARS stays one oversized chunk, which is usually the right trade. Tiny trailing chunks get merged into the previous chunk of the same section, so you don't embed one-line orphans. Stable IDs ( url#index ) let you re-crawl and upsert. Pair them with last_modified to re-embed only pages that changed. From chunks.jsonl , loading into a vector store is one loop: embed embed_text , store text , url , title and heading_path as metadata, and return url with each answer as the citation. Getting the crawl scope right Start at the section you need : https://example.com/docs/ with scope: "path" crawls only /docs/... . Versioned docs: exclude old versions with excludeGlobs: ["**/v1/**"] , or the same answer appears three times with three different version numbers. Paginated listings: excludeGlobs: ["**?page=*"] skips archive pages that are lists of links. Check word_count after a test run of 20 pages. Pages with very few words are often index pages; filter them out before chunking if they add nothing. Limits No JavaScript rendering. It reads the HTML the server sends, which covers most docs sites, blogs, knowledge bases and server-rendered React or Next.js. Client-side-only pages (an empty app shell) are skipped, listed in the log and not charged. HTML only. PDFs, images and other files are skipped. One site per start URL. www. and the bare domain count as one site; other subdomains aren't followed. Speed. At most two new requests per second per site, slower when robots.txt sets a Crawl-delay. Conversion is CPU-bound: the README measures about 1,000 large documentation pages an hour at 256 MB, so the default one-hour run fits roughly 1,000 to 3,000 pages. The run stops itself before its timeout and keeps the pages done so far. Pages over 2 MB of HTML are skipped and not charged. Main-content detection is automatic , so on unusual layouts a little boilerplate can remain or a side block can be dropped. Spot-check a few pages. Robots.txt is always obeyed and can't be turned off. Pages behind logins, paywalls or bot challenges aren't accessible. Crawl only sites you have the right to use this way. Copyright in the content stays with its owner. Crawls a whole site at 256 MB, robots.txt always obeyed, failed, duplicate and empty pages never charged. Not offered: JavaScript rendering, which both Apify Actors have. Cost At the time of writing, the README lists $1.50 per 1,000 pages on Apify's free plan and $1.05 per 1,000 on paid plans (Bronze, Silver, Gold), plus $0.001 per run. Skipped pages (robots.txt, errors, non-HTML, duplicate URLs or identical Markdown, JavaScript-only pages, pages with no main content) aren't charged. The 100-page example costs at most $0.15. title: How to balance AI cost with user intent (1)
author: XJTLU media
summary: You don't always select the best model for users when they simply want to ask "Hi, what is your model?" Therefore, you want to build a LLM router inside your AI app, which can save tons of premium tokens output for simple questions. An AI LLM router is fundamentally a decision engine that maps: user intent + constraints + economics + risk + context → optimal model/tool/workflow execution path Core Architecture The core architecture of an AI router is User Input Gateway authentication Token Introspection & Cryptographic Verification: Validate incoming JWTs or API keys at the API gateway layer (e.g., Envoy, Kong, or a custom Rust/Go middleware) using RS256/EdDSA public keys. rate limiting Context Hydration: Upon validation, extract the tenant_id, user_id, and tier (e.g., free, premium, enterprise). Inject these into the request context header (X-Tenant-ID, X-User-Tier). This tiering is crucial for downstream routing. Distributed Rate Limiting: Implement a Redis-backed Token Bucket or Leaky Bucket algorithm to prevent cascading failures. Multi-Dimensional Limits: Evaluate rate limits across three concurrent vectors: IP/User ID: Prevents DDoS and brute-force abuse. Tier-based Concurrency: Limits maximum active concurrent requests (e.g., 50 concurrent requests for Premium, 5 for Free).Estimated Token Throughput: A rough, pre-routing heuristic calculation (e.g., based on input character count: $\text{characters} \times 0.25$) to drop requests that exceed a tenant's rolling minute-by-minute token quota before hitting expensive models. request normalization Strict Serialization: Enforce an OpenAPI 3.0/JSON Schema validation layer using high-performance validators (e.g., Pydantic in Python, Ajv in Node.js). Structure Alignment: Sanitize heterogenous client payloads into a strict, unified internal schema (e.g., mapping various client formats into a standardized {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "..."}], "generation_params": {}} structure). streaming Protocol Management: Support both Server-Sent Events (SSE, text/event-stream) and WebSockets for duplex or persistent connections. Asynchronous Proxying: The gateway must support HTTP chunked transfer encoding, allowing it to proxy tokens from downstream LLMs to the client with sub-10ms overhead. This requires an asynchronous network stack (e.g., Tokyo/Rust or Asyncio/Python) to hold open connections without thread exhaustion. session tracking Session Windowing: Extract a session_id or conversation_id. If missing, generate a UUIDv4. State Hydration: Query a low-latency cache (Redis or Aerospike) to fetch the sliding window history of the conversation. Context Windows Management: Track total accumulated tokens in the session history. If the history exceeds a threshold, execute a deterministic truncation or summarization strategy before passing it to the preprocessing layer, saving downstream parsing overhead. metadata enrichment Network & Client Fingerprinting: Inject metadata including client_geo (via MaxMind GeoIP), device_type, request_timestamp_utc, and network latency metrics. Routing Hints: Append historical model preferences for this specific user (e.g., if the user always toggles "Creative Mode", append a metadata flag preferred_track: creative). Preprocessing Layer To prevent noisy, malformed inputs from degrading embedding quality or tricking downstream intent classifiers, the text must be cleaned deterministically. Typo Correction (Heuristic vs. Light Neural): Avoid heavy LLMs here due to cost. Use a fast, symmetric delete spelling correction algorithm (SymSpell) or a lightweight, localized character-level sequence-to-sequence model for domain-specific terms. Purpose: Correcting "fiannce" to "finance" significantly stabilizes downstream embedding vectors. Language Detection: Route text through ultra-fast, compiled sub-millisecond classifiers like FastText (Facebook) or CLD3. Routing Relevance: Non-English inputs might require specialized multilingual models (e.g., Cohere, Qwen, or deep-seek variants) that possess superior tokenization efficiency and semantic understanding for that specific language, minimizing token bloat caused by poor subword tokenization. Formatting Cleanup: Regex-based stripping of control characters, unwanted ANSI escape codes, duplicate whitespaces, and systematic markdown/HTML stripping (unless structural layout is explicitly needed). Normalize unicode normalization forms (e.g., converting to NFKC) to ensure identical characters have identical byte representations. Domain Detection: Run the input text through a fast, linear classifier or a lightweight distilled transformer (e.g., a fine-tuned DistilBERT) trained on your target domains (e.g., code, legal, medical, general_chitchat). Cost Balancing: If the domain is general_chitchat, the router immediately flags this for a sub-billion parameter model ($0.07/M tokens), completely bypassing frontier models. Entity Recognition (NER): Deploy a high-throughput spaCy pipeline or a fine-tuned GLiNER model to extract named entities (ORG, PRODUCT, GPE, DATE). PII Masking & Compliance: If sensitive PII (e.g., SSN, CREDIT_CARD) is detected, trigger token masking/anonymization filters before the request is sent to external, third-party closed-source APIs. User Intent Hints: Utilize pattern-matching state machines combined with a multi-label classification head to detect explicit structural intents: requires_calculation, requires_code_generation, complex_reasoning, factual_retrieval. Example: If the intent matches requires_calculation, the router can flag the request to bypass standard LLMs and route directly to an agent with a Python REPL tool, or a model with native tool-calling optimizations. Embeddings Generation:Pass the normalized text to a highly efficient, local embedding model running on a dedicated inference server. Calculate deterministic lexical metrics: Token Count (using specific tokenizers like TikToken for OpenAI, or LlamaTokenizer), character-to-token ratios, sentence count, tree-depth parsing metrics, and the frequency of structural markers (e.g., brackets, assignment operators =, SQL keywords). Extract abstract conceptual indicators: Sentiment polarity score (via VADER or high-speed transformer), perplexity estimation (using a tiny causal model like GPT (to minimize cost) to evaluate how "predictable" or standard the user's phrasing is), and information density (ratio of content words to stop words).

title: How we made a small stationery site readable to AI assistants
author: Ellis
summary: AI-assistance disclosure: this post was drafted with an AI assistant and edited by the person who runs the site. I run Stationery Times, an independent stationery reference with no affiliate links. Stationery Times is a static Astro site of sourced guides to pens, inks, paper, notebooks and planners. We wanted AI assistants to be able to read it and cite it correctly. These are the things we built, and nothing here is a guarantee of citations. Answer first. Every guide opens with a 40 to 60 word direct answer and 4 to 5 takeaways. Headings are phrased as the question a person would ask, and each is answered in a bold first sentence. Plain text twins. Each guide has a Markdown copy at the same address with .md on the end, and the server returns Markdown when a client sends Accept: text/markdown . We also publish /llms.txt and /llms-full.txt . Structured data that matches the page. BlogPosting , Product , FAQPage and BreadcrumbList markup is generated from the same data as the visible text, and a build check fails if the schema and the page disagree. Tell crawlers when something changes. We ping IndexNow on every deploy, keep an RSS feed, and our robots.txt allows the major AI crawlers. Build gates. The build fails on answers that are too long, links to missing anchors, future dates and missing Markdown twins, so the rules hold as the page count grows. What we cannot say yet. We have no hands-on test photos, and some guides still lean on sources we plan to replace. We list what we verify with makers and mark what we could not confirm. If you want to see how it looks in practice, the Japan vs US price index is a good example of a data page with an open CSV.

title: How to Structure a WordPress Site So Google (and Visitors) Understand It
author: MSDevSEO
summary: Most WordPress sites do not have a traffic problem — they have a structure problem. Pages are added one at a time, menus grow without a plan, and after a year the site is a maze: Google cannot tell which page matters most, and visitors cannot find the service they came for. A clear structure fixes both problems at once, and it costs nothing except a little planning. Think of your site as a small shop, not a warehouse. A shop has a front door (the homepage), a few clear sections (services, about, contact), and shelves inside each section. A warehouse has everything piled together. Your homepage should link to your main service pages, and each service page should link back to the homepage and sideways to related services. When every page links to every other page in a giant footer menu, nothing stands out — Google treats all pages as equally important, which means none of them is. Start with five to eight main pages and no more. For a typical small business in Pakistan, that means: home, two to four service pages (one per real service, not one page listing everything), about, blog, and contact. If you offer ten services, group them: "Web Design," "SEO," and "Maintenance" as main pages, with the details underneath. A visitor who lands on your SEO page should immediately see what SEO includes, who it is for, and how to enquire — not a wall of text about your whole company. URLs matter more than people think. A clean URL like /website-development-services/ tells both Google and a human what the page is about. A URL full of numbers, dates, and random words tells nobody anything. When you create a page in WordPress, check its permalink before publishing, and keep it short, readable, and stable — changing URLs later breaks links and loses rankings. Internal links are the quiet ranking tool most small sites ignore. Every new blog post should link to the one or two service pages it relates to, using natural words as the link text — not "click here." Over months, those links tell Google which pages you consider most important, and they guide real visitors from reading an article to making an enquiry. That is the whole point of a blog: not traffic for its own sake, but a path from useful content to a service page. Finally, prune. If a page has had no visits and no purpose for a year, it is not harmless — it dilutes the rest of the site. Either update it with a real purpose or remove it and redirect it to the closest live page. A smaller, well-organised site almost always outperforms a larger, messy one. At MSDevSEO ( https://msdevseo.com/ ), we build WordPress sites with this structure from day one — clear sections, clean URLs, and internal links that lead visitors toward an enquiry instead of a dead end. If your site has grown into a maze, our website development services ( https://msdevseo.com/website-development-services/ ) include a structure cleanup as part of a redesign, so both Google and your customers can finally find what matters.

title: One availability read per house: how my open-source coworking template books a whole day
author: Stan
summary: A coworking member's day is rarely one booking. It's a desk from nine, a meeting room for the 11 o'clock, and somewhere quiet for a call at two. Most booking widgets sell those one at a time: three flows, three checkouts, three confirmation emails. Gable is the open-source Next.js template I built to sell the day instead. It's a coworking site for a made-up network of six buildings in Dublin, Cork and Galway, with 77 bookable spaces, and the whole design is drawn like an architect's drawing set. This post is about the parts I'd copy into any multi-resource booking site: how it reads availability, why the browser does the maths, and how it suggests what your day is missing without calling an API. Live demo · GitHub (MIT) · the longer write-up The cart is a day sheet The planner at /book is a search, not a wizard. You pick a house, a day, how long, a start time and how many people, and you get the spaces that fit, each with a day bar where booked time is hatched like a cut wall in a drawing. Whatever you add lands on the day sheet on the right, which is the cart drawn as a timeline from 08:00 to 20:00. Each booking is held for 15 minutes while you plan the rest, so the room you picked first is still yours when you go back for a desk. Checkout happens once, for everything. The planner state lives in the URL ( /book?house=dock-house&kind=room&date=…&start=10:00&length=60&people=6 ), so a link from the home page or a space page lands on the exact search. One availability read per house, not one per space per day Every space in Gable is its own resource: a room, a booth, a studio desk. The booking API answers availability per space. The naive version of this page asks for every space, for the selected day, every time you change the day, and with 77 spaces across six houses and a 21-day window, that gets expensive fast. Gable flips it. The server asks each space once for its merged free ranges across the whole booking horizon (no date parameter), caches each space for 60 seconds, and sends the browser one response per house. This is lib/availability-server.ts , trimmed: async function readRanges ( spaceId : string , houseId : string , tz : string ): Promise < Packed [] > { for ( let attempt = 0 ; ; attempt ++ ) { try { // throwOnError is required: without it the SDK resolves a 429 as an empty result. const { data } = await ProductService . getCurrentAvailabilitiesMerged ({ path : { productId : spaceId }, query : { locationId : houseId , timezone : tz }, throwOnError : true , }); const until = nowMin () + ( WINDOW_DAYS + 1 ) * 1440 ; return mergePacked (( data ?? []). map ( pack )). filter (([ s , len ]) => len > 0 && s < until ); } catch ( err ) { const status = err instanceof OpencalsApiError ? err . status : 0 ; const retriable = status === 429 || status === 503 || status === 0 ; if ( ! retriable || attempt >= MAX_RETRIES ) throw err ; await sleep ( 400 * 2 ** attempt + Math . floor ( Math . random () * 250 )); } } } function cachedRanges ( spaceId : string , houseId : string , tz : string ) { return unstable_cache (() => readRanges ( spaceId , houseId , tz ), [ ' space-ranges-v1 ' , spaceId , houseId , tz ], { revalidate : 60 , tags : [ ' availability ' , `space: ${ spaceId } ` , `house: ${ houseId } ` ], })(); } Three details in there cost me time: That throwOnError comment is real. Without it, a rate-limited request resolves as an empty list, and an empty list looks exactly like "fully booked". You'd show a house as full because you asked too fast. The reads run three at a time , with exponential backoff and jitter on 429 and 503. A space that still fails isn't cached; it goes into a failed list in the response, and the client asks again for just that space a moment later. The cache tags are what keep it honest. A booking drops the space:<id> tag for that space; a cancel, a move or a cart removal drops the house. So the 60-second cache never shows a slot as free after someone took it through this site. The browser does the maths Each free range is packed into a tuple, [start, length, taken, capacity] , in UTC epoch minutes. For a meeting room taken is 0 and capacity is 1. For the open-plan flex floor, which is one product with 40 seats, taken is the peak number of seats already booked over that span. export type Packed = [ start : number , length : number , taken : number , capacity : number ]; /** Seats still free for the whole of [start, start + minutes] (0 when it doesn't fit). */ export function seatsLeft ( ranges : Packed [] | undefined , start : number , minutes : number ): number { const r = covering ( ranges , start , minutes ); return r ? Math . max ( 0 , r [ 3 ] - r [ 2 ]) : 0 ; } export function fits ( ranges : Packed [] | undefined , start : number , minutes : number , seats = 1 ): boolean { return seatsLeft ( ranges , start , minutes ) >= Math . max ( 1 , seats ); } Everything on the planner comes from those few functions: which spaces fit, "Free at 10:00", "Next free 14:30", "23 seats free", the start times, the day strip. Changing the day, the length, the start or the number of people never calls the API. Two small things worth knowing if you do this yourself. The API can split one free range at a one-second seam, so mergePacked joins spans that touch. And because the merged range reports the peak seats taken, "seats left" is conservative: it may say 22 when 23 are free for part of the span, never the other way round. "Fits in your day" runs without a single API call Under the day sheet there's a short list of suggestions, and it's my favourite part of the template: a desk around your meetings, on the same floor, a phone booth in the half hour between two meetings, lunch or coffee for the number of people in a room, a bigger room that's free at the same time, when your guest list is close to the room's seats, parking at the houses that have it. All of it is lib/upsell.ts , computed from what's already on the sheet and the ranges the browser already holds. The booth one is the whole idea in eight lines: // 3. A booth in a gap const booths = houseSpaces . filter (( s ) => s . kind === ' booth ' ); for ( let i = 0 ; i < today . length - 1 && booths . length ; i ++ ) { const gapStart = today [ i ] ! . end ; const gapEnd = today [ i + 1 ] ! . start ; if ( gapEnd - gapStart < 30 ) continue ; const booth = booths . find (( s ) => fits ( ranges [ s . id ], gapStart , 30 )); if ( booth ) { out . push ({ key : `booth: ${ gapStart } ` , type : ' add ' , space : booth , start : gapStart , minutes : 30 , price : priceFor ( booth , 30 ), title : ' A booth between meetings ' , note : ` ${ booth . name } is free for that half hour` }); break ; } } Every suggestion is checked with fits() before it's shown, so it never offers a booth that's taken. Same key setup as the other templates Gable calls the API from its own server, so it uses a private storefront key ( spk_ ) and forwards each visitor's IP, which means every visitor gets their own rate limit instead of all of them sharing your server's: // lib/opencals.ts import { setupOpencals } from ' @opencals/storefront-sdk ' ; import { nextBuyerIp } from ' @opencals/storefront-sdk/next ' ; setupOpencals ({ baseUrl : process . env . OPENCALS_API_URL ?? ' https://api.opencals.com ' , apiKey : process . env . OPENCALS_API_KEY , // spk_… buyerIp : nextBuyerIp , }); The confirmation is a drawing of the building After checkout, /thank-you draws a section through the house, with each booked space on its floor and a dashed route from the front door, next to a title block with the date, the bookings, the total and how you're paying. It prints as a one-page day sheet with the site chrome hidden. The account opens on a Week plan rather than a list, because coworking members book in patterns: Monday and Thursday at a desk, the same room every Tuesday. Desks are hatched, rooms are solid, and each upcoming booking has Change time, Stay longer, Invite and Cancel. Where it stops So you don't find out after you've forked it: No monthly memberships or credit allowances. Gable is pay-as-you-go. If your coworking space runs on "10 room hours included" plans, you need a membership system alongside it. Memberships are in beta on the Opencals side. No doors, Wi-Fi or printers. It collects a meeting name "for the door screen" at checkout, and that's as far as it goes into the building. No webhooks yet. Booking events reach other tools through Zapier. The engine isn't open source. The template, the SDK and the agent skills are MIT. Availability, holds, payments and accounts run on Opencals, which is a hosted service and the thing I build. The free development store has every feature in test mode, but it can't take real payments. Running your own copy Sign up at app.opencals.com , create a Dev Store in Ireland (the store's country sets the currency) and choose the Gable (Coworking) dataset. It seeds the six houses, 77 spaces, 16 extras, three discounts and the checkout questions. Create a private storefront key ( spk_ ) in the dashboard. Deploy with the Vercel button in the README, setting OPENCALS_API_KEY and AUTH_SECRET . To check the screens after booking without making a booking, run it locally and open /preview , which renders them from fixtures built from your catalogue. The previous post in this series was the Haar salon template rebuild . If you build something on Gable, or think the one-read-per-house approach breaks somewhere I haven't hit yet, I'd like to hear it in the comments.

title: Designing Power-Ups Around a Theme: The Hydro Robot Runner
author: Instant Games
summary: Power-ups are easy to add and hard to make meaningful. A speed boost, a shield, a magnet: every runner has them. In AI Rush, a free 3D endless runner you play in the browser, I tried to let the theme decide what the power-ups are. This post is about that process. The premise You play Hydro AI, a robot running through a smart city. Obstacles are lasers, drones, security bots and rolling power cells. The robot runs on water and electricity, so the power-ups come from those two resources. When the theme and mechanics share a vocabulary, players learn faster. Nobody needs a tutorial to guess what "Hydro Shield" does. Two resources, four power-ups You collect water and electricity as you run. Those feed four effects: Hydro Shield protects you from a hit. Lightning Dash gets you through danger quickly. Water Jet clears the way ahead. Battery Overdrive boosts your run. I like this structure for a reason: collecting two simple things creates choice. A runner that offers one pickup type gives you no decisions. A runner with a dozen overwhelms. Two resources and four outcomes is a small enough space to understand and big enough to feel clever. Obstacles that teach Each obstacle should demand a slightly different response, otherwise they are just reskins of the same hazard. Lasers read as "go around or through the gap." Drones move, so they demand timing. Security bots occupy space, so they push you to change lane. Rolling power cells come at you, so they reward a quick reaction. If every obstacle asks the same question, the game gets dull quickly. Unlocks as a long-term goal There are 4 unlockable robots. Unlocks matter in an endless runner because there is no final level. They give a reason to keep going even when a personal best is out of reach. Why "3D" in the browser Players searching for 3D endless runner games or 3D running games are often disappointed by pages that need a plugin or a download. AI Rush runs in the browser with no install. That constraint pushed me to keep scenes light and the obstacle set readable at speed on a phone. Takeaways Let the theme name the mechanics. Keep the resource space small. Make each hazard ask a different question. Give endless games something to unlock. Try it AI Rush is free to play in the browser , with no sign-up. What is the best power-up system you have seen in a runner? AI Rush is also one of the hyper casual games in the catalog: quick play games that start instantly and reward practice.

title: AIエージェントの非同期ツール呼び出し：なぜブロッキングなrun()よりstart()が優れているのか
author: Akira
summary: 要点： AIエージェントの非同期ツール呼び出し（Async Tool Calls）は、ブロッキングな1回の run() をシンプルに分割した仕組みです。 start() ですぐにジョブハンドルを返し、 status() で進捗を報告し、 stop() でキャンセルを実行。処理結果は後からイベントとして返され、エージェントは次のターンでそれを読み取ります。これにより、時間のかかるタスクの実行中でも、エージェントは対話を続け、新たな指示を受け付けられます。 今すぐApidogを試す 現在の多くのエージェントは、ツールを呼び出すと完了するまで待機します。6分かかるテストの実行中に別の質問を投げても、キューで待たされることになります。200ミリ秒で終わる検索なら問題ありませんが、デプロイやWebクローリングのような重いタスクでは大きなストレスになります。 DeepSeek Harnessチームが公開した最新のエッセイ 「Exploring Super-agent Design（スーパーエージェント設計の探求）」 では、この解決策を「全二重（full-duplex）」と呼んでいます。ブロッキングな run() をやめ、 start() と stop() に置き換えるアプローチです。本ガイドでは、ツール仕様、結果のフィードバック、キャンセル処理、各ツールに必要なAPI設計など、エージェントループ側の実装を解説します。時間のかかる単一呼び出しにおけるHTTP側の実装については、 「AIエージェントと長時間実行API：ポーリング vs Webhook」 をご覧ください。 エージェントループにおける非同期ツール呼び出しとは？ 非同期ツール呼び出しとは、結果の代わりにハンドルを即座に返すツール実行方式です。エージェントループはハンドルを記録してターンを終了し、ユーザーからの入力待ち状態を解放します。処理が完了すると、ランタイムが完了イベントを会話履歴に注入し、モデルは次のターンで通常のメッセージと同様にそれを読み取ります。 最大の違いは「誰が待つか」です。 run() ではモデルが待機しますが、 start() ではランタイム側が待機します。 ブロッキング run() 非同期 start() 返り値 最終結果 ジョブID、「Started」 処理中のエージェント フリーズ（応答不可） 対話、計画、追加ジョブの開始が可能 新規ユーザーメッセージ ツールの処理完了までキューで待機 即座に処理 キャンセル ターン全体を強制終了 stop(job_id) DeepSeekのエッセイでは、これを完成した製品機能ではなくアーキテクチャの青写真として説明しています。全二重機能はDeepSeek Harness内に実装されているもののデフォルトでは有効になっておらず、一部は dsh-superagent-prototype というプロトタイププラグイン（著者曰くDeepSeekの公式製品ではないとのこと）に含まれています。これは参考とすべき設計パターンとして捉えるのがよいでしょう。背景については、 DeepSeek Harnessの解説記事 や、関連記事の スーパーエージェントの構築方法 をご覧ください。 ブロッキングの課題：1つの重いツールがエージェント全体を停止させる テストスイートの実行（5分）と、インポートエラーに関する質問への回答をコーディングエージェントに依頼した場面を想像してみてください。ブロッキングな呼び出しの場合、質問の回答にテスト結果が不要であっても、質問はテストが完了するまで待たされます。その結果、次の3つの問題が生じます。 レイテンシの累積： 実行に時間のかかるツールがあるたびに、その所要時間すべてが後続の処理の待ち時間に上乗せされます。 指示の陳腐化： 開始2分後に「やっぱりe2eテストはスキップして」と伝えても、エージェントはテストが終わるまでその指示を認識できません。 タイムアウトの発生： 数分間にわたって接続を開いたままにするとゲートウェイによって切断されるため、バックグラウンドの処理自体は成功していても、長時間の run() がエラーになることがあります。 エージェントに求められるこの特性を、エッセイでは「プロダクティブ（高生産的）」と呼んでいます。前の処理が終わるのを待たずに次の指示を受け付けられる状態のことです。非同期ツールを使えば、これを実現できます。 start、status、stop：非同期ツールのインターフェース仕様 時間のかかる機能ごとに、1つの巨大なツールではなく、返り値のデータ構造がコンパクトな3つのツールをモデルに提供します。 { "name" : "start_test_run" , "description" : "Start the test suite. Returns immediately with a job_id. The result arrives later as a job_completed event; do not wait for it." , "input_schema" : { "type" : "object" , "properties" : { "suite" : { "type" : "string" , "enum" : [ "unit" , "e2e" , "all" ] }, "idempotency_key" : { "type" : "string" } }, "required" : [ "suite" , "idempotency_key" ] } } start_test_run は {"job_id": "job_8f2", "status": "queued"} のみを返します。 get_job_status(job_id) は、簡単な進捗メッセージに加えて queued 、 running 、 done 、または failed を返します。 stop_job(job_id) はキャンセルを要求し、到達したステータスを返します。 モデルを正しく動作させるための2つの鉄則があります。1つは、ツールの説明文に「待機しないこと（do not wait）」と明記することです。そうしないと、モデルは get_job_status を小刻みにポーリングし続けてしまいます。もう1つは、 start から処理結果のデータを返さないことです。返してしまうと、モデルがどの形式のレスポンスを受け取ったのか推測しなければならなくなります。 処理結果をエージェントループにフィードバックする仕組み モデル自身によるポーリングは最終手段であり、推奨される設計ではありません。より優れたアプローチは、ランタイムがジョブを監視し、新しいメッセージとして完了イベントを会話にプッシュすることです。 [event] job_completed job_id=job_8f2 tool=start_test_run status=done summary: 412 passed, 3 failed (auth/session.test.ts) details: get_job_result(job_8f2) イベントの内容は簡潔に保ち、詳細なペイロードは取得ツール経由で取得できるようにしておきます。こうすることで、4万行にも及ぶログがコンテキストを圧迫するのを防げます。 次に重要なのがバッチ処理です。DeepSeekのエッセイでは、1回のターン中に発生したトリガーを集約し、次のモデル呼び出しにまとめて組み込むルーターについて説明されています。長い入力と短い出力をプリフィル（prefill）に折り込むアプローチです。同チームの実験では、1分あたりのトリガー数が1件から40件に増加し、平均バッチサイズは1.0から2.8に拡大、1回の判断にかかる時間は6.4秒から1.6秒へと短縮されました。これらは一般的なベンチマークではなく論文内の実験値ですが、3つのイベントを個別に3回呼び出して処理するより、1回の呼び出しでまとめて処理するほうが効率的であることは明らかです。基本ルールはシンプルです。モデルの生成中はイベントとユーザーメッセージをキューに溜めておき、ターンが終了した段階で到着順にまとめて送信します。 実行順序の制御、キャンセル処理、冪等性キー 実行順序： ジョブはどのような順序で完了するかわかりません。ジョブBがジョブAに依存している場合は、ジョブAの完了イベントを受け取ってからジョブBを開始するか、API側で depends_on を受け付けるようにして、依存関係を明示的に管理します。 キャンセル処理： stop はあくまで停止要求であり、確約ではありません。実際の最終ステータス（ cancelled 、あるいは先に完了していた場合は done ）を返し、モデルがそれを正確に報告できるようにします。MCPのTasks拡張機能も同様のスタンスをとっており、ドキュメントではキャンセルを協調的（cooperative）なものと位置づけているため、タスクが cancelled 以外の完了ステータスに達する可能性があります。 冪等性キー： モデルは再試行を行うことがあるため、レスポンスが途切れた場合に2回目の start が実行される恐れがあります。すべての start で idempotency_key を必須とし、同じキーを受け取った場合は既存のジョブを返すようにAPIを設計します。これがないと、「マイグレーションの実行」などが誤って2度実行されるリスクがあります。 中間結果の取得： 全体の完了を待つのではなく、 get_job_result(job_id, cursor) などを通じて初期の出力（クロールした最初の50ページなど）を取得できるようにします。 コンテキスト肥大化の防止： 完了したジョブは、モデルが処理した段階で1行のサマリーに圧縮します。 タイムアウト： 各ジョブに期限を設定し、超過した場合は job_timed_out を発行します。 バックエンドAPIに必要な要件 非同期ツールの品質は、背後にあるジョブAPIの出来栄えに左右されます。処理を受け付け、IDを返し、呼び出し元が進捗を確認できるようにする設計が必要です。 RFC 9110では202 Accepted を「リクエストは処理のために受理されたが、処理は完了していない」と定義しており、 MDNの202解説ページ ではその実践的な使用法が説明されています。 start() ツール向けの最小限のジョブAPI仕様： 呼び出し レスポンス 使用箇所 POST /jobs （ Idempotency-Key ヘッダー付き） 202 + {"job_id", "status":"queued"} + Location: /jobs/{id} start GET /jobs/{id} 200 + queued , running , done または failed status 、ジョブ監視機能 GET /jobs/{id}/result 出力付き 200 、未完了の場合は 409 取得ツール DELETE /jobs/{id} キャンセル要求を受け付ける 202 （以降の呼び出しでは 404 または 409 ） stop 任意のコールバックURL 完了時に呼び出し元へ POST ジョブ監視機能 このコールバックにより、ランタイムはポーリングを行わずにイベントをプッシュできるようになります。どちらを採用すべきか迷った場合は、 Webhook vs ポーリング でトレードオフを解説しています。また、イベント駆動型APIについては AsyncAPIとは何か で詳しく取り上げています。 ツールがMCP（Model Context Protocol）に対応しているなら、すでに標準仕様が存在します。 MCP仕様（バージョン 2026-07-28） では、オプションの拡張機能として Tasks が定義されています。サーバーは tools/call に対して taskId を含む CreateTaskResult で応答でき、クライアントは tasks/get をポーリング（または notifications/tasks を受信）し、 tasks/cancel で停止を要求します。ステータスには working 、 input_required 、 completed 、 failed 、 cancelled があります。クライアントとサーバーの双方が対応している必要があり、ホスト側のサポート状況も異なるため、依存する前にクライアントの対応状況を確認してください。 Apidog CLIを使ってコーディングエージェントにジョブAPIを構築・テストさせる ジョブAPIは、エージェントを実際に動かす前に検証可能な部分です。設計とテストをコーディングエージェントに任せ、 Apidog CLI を操作させましょう。プロンプトを1つ作成するだけで、エージェントが仕様の策定からテストケースの作成、実行まで行います。 セットアップはわずか3つのコマンドで完了します： npm install -g apidog-cli@latest apidog auth login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN> npx -y skills add https://apidog.com # pick your agent when prompted 続いて、エージェントに次のようなプロンプトを与えます： In Apidog project <projectId>, design the job API a start() tool needs: POST /jobs returns 202 with job_id, GET /jobs/{id} returns queued|running|done|failed, DELETE /jobs/{id} cancels. Create the endpoints, then create test cases that assert: 202 and a job_id on create, a status that reaches done within 60 seconds, the same job_id when the Idempotency-Key repeats, and 409 or 404 on GET result after cancel. Run them against the staging environment <envId> and summarize failures. エージェントはCLIから各ペイロードの構造を読み取って検証し、次のように作成とテストを実行します： apidog cli-schema get endpoint-create apidog cli-schema validate endpoint-create --file post-jobs.json apidog endpoint create --project <projectId> --file post-jobs.json apidog cli-schema get test-case-create apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case -create-202 .json apidog test-case create --project <projectId> --file case -create-202 .json apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <projectId> -e <envId> -r cli,json cli レポーターは各アサーションの合否をターミナルに出力し、 json レポートはエージェントが結果を読み込んで説明するための構造化データを提供します。テストに合格したら、CI環境で -r junit を指定して同じコマンドを実行できます。 Apidog CLIエージェントワークフローガイド ではこの一連の流れを詳しく解説しており、 Claude CodeでのApidog CLI活用法 ではエージェントの設定方法を取り上げています。なお、ApidogのFreeプランは最大4ユーザーまで利用可能です。 非同期ツールを採用すべきケースと不要なケース 非同期ツールを使うべきケース： ツールの実行に通常数秒以上かかる場合（ビルド、テストスイート、クローリング、レンダリング、デプロイなど）。 処理の実行中にもユーザーがエージェントと対話する場合。 ブロッキングのままでよいケース： 呼び出しが1〜2秒未満で返ってくる場合。 どのみち結果が得られなければ次のステップを開始できない場合。 本物のジョブAPIを用意できない場合（内部で同期的にブロックする疑似非同期ツールは、無駄に複雑さを増すだけです）。 実践的な使い分けとしては、読み取り処理はブロッキングのままにし、長時間の書き込みや重い計算処理を非同期にするのが適切です。 よくある質問（FAQ） 非同期ツール呼び出しと並列ツール呼び出しの違いは何ですか？ 並列ツール呼び出し（Parallel Tool Calls）は、1回のターン内で複数のツールを同時に実行しますが、モデルはすべての処理が完了するまで待機します。一方、非同期ツール呼び出しは即座に応答を返し、後続のターンにまたがって完了するため、処理の実行中もモデルは対話を継続できます。 非同期ツールを構築するにはMCPが必須ですか？ いいえ、必須ではありません。ジョブIDを返すツールと、完了イベントを注入できるランタイムがあれば機能します。MCPのTasks拡張機能（オプション）は、クライアントとサーバーの双方がサポートしている場合に、ハンドル管理、ポーリング、キャンセル処理などの標準化を提供してくれるものです。 エージェントはジョブの完了をどのように検知しますか？ ランタイムがエージェントに通知します。ジョブ監視機能がジョブAPIをポーリングするかコールバックを受信し、簡潔な完了イベントを会話履歴に追加します。モデルは次のターンでそれを読み取ります。 ジョブの途中でユーザーがキャンセルした場合はどうなりますか？ エージェントが stop(job_id) を呼び出し、APIがリクエストを記録して、ジョブが実際の最終ステータスを報告します。キャンセルの要求が届く前に処理が完了していた場合は、中断されたと偽るのではなく、完了したことをエージェントが正確に伝える必要があります。 DeepSeekの全二重（full-duplex）モードは設定でオンにできますか？ 製品の正式機能としては提供されていません。エッセイによるとDeepSeek Harnessに実装されているもののデフォルトでは無効になっており、関連するプラグインも公式製品ではないプロトタイプとされています。参考となるリファレンス設計として活用してください。

title: I added Magic Pen to PeepNote: draw around screen content and ask AI
author: AlexYoo
summary: In my previous post , I introduced PeepNote, a desktop app for keeping useful LLM answers and finding them again while working. This time, I added Magic Pen to make asking the next question easier. While reading documentation or browsing a website, I often find something I want an AI to explain. Usually, that means copying text or taking a screenshot, opening a chat, and pasting everything there. I wanted to make that process shorter. Draw around what you want to understand Press Alt+S and draw around part of your screen. Magic Pen sends the selected area to your configured AI and opens a movable window with a streaming response. You can use it to understand a diagram, explain unfamiliar terminology, or organize information from a document. For example, while reading about RAG, you could select an architecture diagram and then ask: How is RAG different from a regular chatbot? Compare them in a simple table. Keep the conversation going The Reply button lets you continue in two ways: Text: type a follow-up question. Magic Pen: select another area and include it in the same conversation. When the explanation is worth keeping, choose a workspace and click Save . The conversation becomes a Markdown note in PeepNote. Choose your AI Magic Pen supports your configured AI API or an installed, signed-in CLI tool: Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, or Qwen Code. You can choose the mode and model in Settings. Selected screen content is sent to the AI service you use, while saved notes stay on your computer. PeepNote is free, open source, and available for Windows and Linux. Website and demo GitHub What would you use a screen-selection AI tool for? I’d love to hear your feedback and ideas for making it more useful.

title: We are witnessing a fundamental shift in the relationship between humans and technology.
author: Esmail Sarhadi
summary: We are witnessing a fundamental shift in the relationship between humans and technology. For decades, we treated technology as a tool — something that could only be useful when guided by our own thinking, decisions, and actions. But AI is challenging that definition. We are moving toward a world where the human role is no longer necessarily to build, code, design, or even figure out how to solve a problem. Instead, we define the objective. AI receives the goal. It analyzes the problem. It develops a plan. It executes the work. And eventually, it delivers the result. Want a website? Describe it. Need an application? Define what it should do. Building an industrial solution? Explain the requirements. The system can increasingly handle the complexity behind the request. And perhaps the most uncomfortable part of this transformation is that we are no longer talking about AI simply making humans more productive. We are talking about AI gradually taking over tasks that once required human expertise, experience, and execution. The real question is no longer whether AI will change our jobs. The question is whether we are prepared for a world in which the ability to execute is no longer our greatest advantage. The future may belong to those who know what to build, why it matters, and how to define the right goals — not necessarily those who build everything themselves. The transition has already begun. Are we ready to accept it? ArtificialIntelligence #AI #FutureOfWork #AutonomousAgents #Technology #SoftwareEngineering #DigitalTransformation

title: Three agent skills for a brief, a poster, and a consistent visual style
author: 郭帅
summary: A small event makes a useful first exercise for agent skills. You need a one-page brief, a poster, and a style you can reuse in follow-up materials. Give each step its own input and check its output before moving on. Turn rough notes into a brief Use Anthropic’s doc-coauthoring to structure a document with your agent. Supply the audience, goal, raw notes, and constraints. For a book club, ask for a one-page proposal with a clear purpose, a rough agenda, and open questions. Confirm the date, venue, and other details from your notes before treating the brief as final. Make a static poster from the approved brief Anthropic’s canvas-design describes a workflow for static artwork in PNG or PDF. Give it the exact title and event details, the intended dimensions, and a visual direction. Open the exported file and check text, font rendering, spacing, and readability at the intended display size. Carry the same style into a second asset Anthropic’s theme-factory provides preset visual themes. Inspect the examples and choose a palette and typography before styling a second artifact, such as a one-page event recap. Compare both outputs side by side for consistent headings, contrast, and margins. Before running any skill, read its current instructions and license and check that your host supports the required tools. The book club example is an exercise you can try. title: Yapay Zeka Ajanları İçin Asenkron Araç Çağrıları: start() Neden Bloklayan run() Yönteminden Daha İyi?
author: Tobias Hoffmann
summary: Yapay Zeka Ajanları İçin Asenkron Araç Çağrıları: start() Neden Bloklayan run() Yönteminden Daha İyi? Kısa cevap: Yapay zekâ ajanları için asenkron araç çağrıları, engelleyici (blocking) tek bir run() işlemini küçük bir sözleşmeye böler: start() anında bir iş tanıtıcısı (job handle) döndürür, status() ilerlemeyi bildirir, stop() işlemi iptal eder ve sonuç, ajanın bir sonraki turunda okuyacağı bir olay (event) olarak geri gelir. Uzun süren işler arka planda çalışırken ajan konuşmaya ve yeni talimatlar almaya devam eder. Bugün Apidog'u deneyin Günümüzdeki çoğu ajan bir aracı çağırır ve bekler. 6 dakikalık bir test çalıştırması sırasında ikinci bir soru sorduğunuzda bu soru kuyrukta bekler. Bu durum 200 ms süren bir arama için sorun olmasa da bir dağıtım (deploy) veya web tarama (crawl) işlemi için oldukça can sıkıcıdır. DeepSeek Harness ekibinin yakın tarihli "Exploring Super-agent Design" makalesi bu çözümü "full-duplex" (çift yönlü eşzamanlı) olarak adlandırıyor: engelleyici run() çağrısını start() ve stop() ile değiştirmek. Bu rehber, ajan döngüsü (agent loop) tarafını ele almaktadır: araç sözleşmesi, sonuçların sisteme nasıl geri aktığı, iptal işlemleri ve her aracın ihtiyaç duyduğu API yapısı. Tek bir yavaş çağrının HTTP tarafı hakkında bilgi edinmek için AI Agents and Long-Running API Calls: Polling vs Webhooks başlıklı yazıyı okuyabilirsiniz. Bir ajan döngüsünde asenkron araç çağrıları nedir? Asenkron bir araç çağrısı, sonuç yerine bir tanıtıcı (handle) döndüren bir araç çağrımıdır. Ajan döngüsü tanıtıcıyı kaydeder, sırasını tamamlar ve kullanıcı için boşta kalır. İş bittiğinde çalışma zamanı (runtime) konuşmaya bir tamamlanma olayı ekler ve model bunu bir sonraki turunda tıpkı diğer mesajlar gibi okur. Aradaki fark kimin beklediğidir: run() ile model bekler, start() ile ise çalışma zamanı bekler. Engelleyici run() Asenkron start() Döndürülen değer Nihai sonuç İş kimliği (job id), "Başlatıldı" İşlem sırasında ajan Donmuş / kilitli Konuşuyor, planlama yapıyor, yeni işler başlatıyor Yeni kullanıcı mesajı Araç yanıtı dönene kadar kuyrukta bekletilir Anında işlenir İptal Tüm turu sonlandırır stop(job_id) DeepSeek makalesi bunu doğrudan kullanıma sunulmuş hazır bir ayar olarak değil, bir mimari olarak tanımlıyor. Full-duplex yapısının DeepSeek Harness içinde uygulandığını ancak varsayılan olarak etkinleştirilmediğini ve bazı parçalarının yazarların resmi bir DeepSeek ürünü olmadığını belirttiği dsh-superagent-prototype adlı bir prototip eklentide yer aldığını ifade ediyor. Bunu örnek alınacak bir tasarım şablonu olarak değerlendirebilirsiniz. Arka plan bilgisi için DeepSeek Harness nedir başlıklı yazıya ve tamamlayıcı nitelikteki süper ajan nasıl inşa edilir rehberine göz atabilirsiniz. Engelleyici çağrı sorunu: Yavaş çalışan tek bir araç ajanı kilitler Test paketini çalıştırması (5 dakika) ve hatalı bir içe aktarma (import) hakkında bir soruyu yanıtlaması istenen bir kodlama ajanı hayal edin. Engelleyici çağrılarda, sorunuz testlerle hiçbir ilgisi olmamasına rağmen testlerin arkasında bekler. Bu durumda üç temel sorun ortaya çıkar: Gecikmeler üst üste biner. Yavaş çalışan her araç, çalışma süresinin tamamını arkasındaki her şeyin bekleme süresine ekler. Talimatlar güncelliğini yitirir. İki dakika sonra "aslında e2e testlerini atla" dersiniz; ancak ajan işlem tamamlanana kadar bunu algılayamaz. Zaman aşımları sorun yaratır. Ağ geçitleri (gateway) dakikalarca açık tutulan bağlantıları sonlandırır; bu nedenle uzun süren bir run() işlemi, arka plandaki iş başarılı olsa bile başarısızlıkla sonuçlanabilir. Makale, hedeflenen bu özelliği "üretken" (productive) olarak tanımlıyor: ajan, önceki iş bitmeden bir sonraki talimatı alabilir. Bunu sağlamanın yolu ise asenkron araçlardan geçer. start, status, stop: Asenkron araç sözleşmesi Uzun süren her yetenek için modele tek bir araç vermek yerine, minimal dönüş yapılarına sahip üç araç sağlayın. { "name" : "start_test_run" , "description" : "Start the test suite. Returns immediately with a job_id. The result arrives later as a job_completed event; do not wait for it." , "input_schema" : { "type" : "object" , "properties" : { "suite" : { "type" : "string" , "enum" : [ "unit" , "e2e" , "all" ] }, "idempotency_key" : { "type" : "string" } }, "required" : [ "suite" , "idempotency_key" ] } } start_test_run yalnızca {"job_id": "job_8f2", "status": "queued"} döndürür ve başka hiçbir şey içermez. get_job_status(job_id) çağrısı queued , running , done veya failed durumlarının yanı sıra kısa bir ilerleme notu döndürür. stop_job(job_id) ise iptal talebinde bulunur ve ulaşılan durumu bildirir. Modelin süreci doğru yürütmesini sağlayan iki kural vardır: Açıklamaya "bekleme" (do not wait) ifadesini ekleyin; aksi takdirde model dar bir döngüde sürekli get_job_status sorgusu yapacaktır (polling). Ayrıca start fonksiyonundan asla veri döndürmeyin; aksi takdirde model hangi veri yapısını aldığını tahmin etmek zorunda kalır. Sonuçlar döngüye nasıl geri döner? Modelin sürekli sorgu (polling) yapması birincil plan değil, yalnızca bir yedek plan olmalıdır. Daha iyi bir tasarımda çalışma zamanı işleri izler ve konuşmaya yeni bir mesaj olarak tamamlama olayını iletir (push): [event] job_completed job_id=job_8f2 tool=start_test_run status=done summary: 412 passed, 3 failed (auth/session.test.ts) details: get_job_result(job_8f2) Olay mesajını kısa tutun ve veri yükünün (payload) tamamını ayrı bir getirme (fetch) aracının arkasına yerleştirin; böylece 40.000 satırlık bir günlük (log) asla bağlamı (context) işgal etmez. Ardından toplu işleme (batching) adımına geçin. DeepSeek makalesi, bir tur sırasında gelen tetikleyicileri toplayıp bunları bir sonraki model çağrısında birleştiren bir yönlendirici (router) tanımlıyor; uzun girdi ve kısa çıktı, ön doldurmaya (prefill) dahil ediliyor. Yaptıkları deneyde, dakikadaki tetikleyici sayısı 1'den 40'a çıktı, ortalama toplu işlem boyutu 1,0'dan 2,8'e yükseldi ve karar başına harcanan süre 6,4 saniyeden 1,6 saniyeye düştü. Bu değerler genel bir karşılaştırma testi (benchmark) değil, makalenin kendi test sonuçlarıdır; ancak üç olayı tek seferde okuyan bir çağrı, her biri tek bir olayı okuyan üç çağrıdan her zaman daha verimlidir. Basit bir kural: Model üretim yaparken olayları ve kullanıcı mesajlarını kuyruğa alın; tur sona erdiğinde bunları geliş sırasına göre birlikte gönderin. Sıralama, iptal ve tekillik anahtarları (idempotency keys) Sıralama. İşler herhangi bir sırayla tamamlanabilir. B işi A işine bağlıysa, bağımlılığı açıkça tanımlayın: B'yi yalnızca A'nın tamamlanma olayından sonra başlatın veya API'nin depends_on parametresi kabul etmesini sağlayın. İptal. stop bir garantiden ziyade bir taleptir. Gerçek nihai durumu döndürün ( cancelled veya daha önce bittiyse done ) ve modelin bunu dürüstçe raporlamasını sağlayın. MCP'nin Tasks uzantısı da aynı yaklaşımı benimser: belgelerinde iptal işlemini işbirlikçi (cooperative) olarak tanımlar, bu nedenle bir görev cancelled dışında bir nihai duruma da ulaşabilir. Tekillik anahtarları (Idempotency keys). Modeller yeniden deneme yapabilir; dolayısıyla iletilemeyen bir yanıt ikinci bir start çağrısını tetikleyebilir. Her start çağrısında bir idempotency_key zorunlu kılın ve API'nin aynı anahtarı tekrar gördüğünde mevcut işi döndürmesini sağlayın. Bu anahtar olmadan "veritabanı göçünü çalıştır" komutu iki kez yürütülebilir. Kısmi sonuçlar. Sürecin sonuna kadar beklemek yerine erken çıktıları (örneğin taranan ilk 50 sayfayı) get_job_result(job_id, cursor) aracılığıyla erişilebilir kılın. Bağlam büyümesi. Model tamamlanan işler doğrultusunda aksiyon aldıktan sonra bu işleri tek bir satırda özetleyin. Zaman aşımları. Her işe bir son tarih (deadline) verin ve bu süre aşıldığında job_timed_out uyarısı üretin. Temeldeki API nasıl görünmelidir? Asenkron bir araç, yalnızca arkasındaki iş API'si kadar iyidir: işi kabul et, bir kimlik geri döndür ve çağıranın durumu kontrol etmesine izin ver. RFC 9110, 202 Accepted durum kodunu "istek işlenmek üzere kabul edildi ancak işleme henüz tamamlanmadı" şeklinde tanımlar; MDN'in 202 referansı ise bunun pratik kullanımını ele alır. Bir start() aracı için minimal bir iş API'si: Çağrı Yanıt Kullanan POST /jobs ( Idempotency-Key başlığı ile) 202 + {"job_id", "status":"queued"} + Location: /jobs/{id} start GET /jobs/{id} 200 + queued , running , done veya failed status , iş izleyici (job watcher) GET /jobs/{id}/result Çıktı ile 200 veya tamamlanmadıysa 409 Getirme aracı (fetch tool) DELETE /jobs/{id} 202 iptal talebi alındı; sonraki çağrılarda 404 veya 409 stop İsteğe bağlı geri arama URL'si (callback URL) Tamamlandığında çağırana POST isteği İş izleyici (job watcher) Çalışma zamanının sorgulama yapmak yerine olayları iletmesini (push) sağlayan unsur bu geri aramadır (callback). İkisi arasında seçim yapmak için desteğe ihtiyaç duyarsanız aralarındaki dengeler webhooks vs polling yazısında, olaya dayalı API tarafı ise AsyncAPI nedir yazısında ele alınmaktadır. Araçlarınız MCP protokolünü kullanıyorsa, artık bunun için bir standart mevcut. MCP teknik özellikleri (2026-07-28 sürümü) , Tasks özelliğini isteğe bağlı bir uzantı olarak listeler: Bir sunucu, tools/call çağrısına bir taskId içeren CreateTaskResult ile yanıt verebilir; istemci tasks/get sorgulaması yapar (veya notifications/tasks bildirimlerini dinler) ve tasks/cancel ile durdurma talebinde bulunur. Durumlar working , input_required , completed , failed ve cancelled şeklindedir. Hem istemcinin hem de sunucunun bunu açıkça desteklemesi gerekir ve ana makine (host) desteği değişkenlik gösterebilir; bu nedenle güvenmeden önce istemcinizi kontrol edin. Kodlama ajanınızın iş API'sini Apidog CLI ile oluşturmasını ve test etmesini sağlayın İş API'si, herhangi bir ajan müdahale etmeden önce doğrulayabileceğiniz kısımdır. Tasarımı ve testleri kodlama ajanınıza teslim edin ve Apidog CLI 'ı yönetmesini sağlayın. Siz tek bir prompt yazarsınız; ajan ise şartnameyi ve test senaryolarını yazar, ardından bunları çalıştırır. Kurulum yalnızca üç komut gerektirir: npm install -g apidog-cli@latest apidog auth login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN> npx -y skills add https://apidog.com # pick your agent when prompted Ardından ajanınıza tek bir prompt verin: In Apidog project <projectId>, design the job API a start() tool needs: POST /jobs returns 202 with job_id, GET /jobs/{id} returns queued|running|done|failed, DELETE /jobs/{id} cancels.
